Chapter 5: Facing Inner Conflicts and Finding Identity Through Stories
You know, every kid goes through moments where their feelings just don’t make sense—even to themselves. There’s this constant pull between wanting to be good and suddenly feeling angry, or maybe a bit jealous. Sometimes, you can love someone deeply and still feel a bit of resentment at the same time. And who hasn’t longed to feel special, while also quietly worrying about being left out?
These are the real, messy parts of growing up. But let’s be honest—talking about these feelings isn’t always easy, especially when the adults around us hope we’ll just behave perfectly.
That’s where fairy tales come in. They don’t expect anyone to be flawless. Instead, they give us a world where every kind of feeling has a place—no shame, no judgment. The characters in these stories mess up, act out of jealousy, or struggle with envy. And you know what? The stories don’t try to sweep any of that under the rug. They bring those struggles right into the open, showing us that it’s possible to feel all sorts of things and still find a path forward.
Think about Snow White for a moment. There’s the queen, eaten up by jealousy. Snow White herself, with her innocence. And don’t forget the kindness of the dwarfs. Every part of that story reflects the complicated emotions kids face every day. The queen’s envy? It’s destructive, no doubt. But if you look closer, it’s also something we can all understand, at least a little. The story doesn’t let her off the hook, but it does say, “Hey, these feelings exist.” For a child listening, that’s huge—it means they’re not alone in how they feel.
And then there’s that classic push and pull between loving your parents and wanting to stand on your own. Fairy tales love to explore this. The hero leaves home, faces all kinds of challenges, and eventually comes back—changed, stronger, with a clearer idea of who they are and what matters to them. It’s not just a trip through the woods or across a kingdom; it’s an emotional journey, too.
What’s really special here is that fairy tales don’t lecture or preach. Instead, their characters live out the same struggles real kids face, and in doing so, they open up all kinds of possibilities. The message is simple: it’s okay to feel angry, jealous, or even afraid. Those emotions are just part of being human. But the stories also show that we can move through those feelings, and grow because of them.
Here’s something beautiful—after listening to a story, a child might not be able to say exactly what they’ve learned. But deep down, something shifts. Maybe there’s a little more acceptance, or a bit more hope. The story becomes a quiet mirror, reflecting both the darkness and the light inside. And in that reflection, the child discovers that their struggles aren’t something to hide—they’re just part of finding out who they really are.
